# Tool-Connected Design Environments {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."*
>
> – John Culkin, *Saturday Review* (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** John Culkin, an American media scholar explaining Marshall McLuhan's ideas, originally used this line to describe how our tools inevitably reshape our own practices. In our work, an architecture tool similarly defines what a given method can tweak and what we can actually observe. If an AI-assisted method drives that tool, we must explicitly declare those limits.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What exactly do we need to wrap around real architecture tools so that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted method can drive them safely, reproducibly, and strictly within our declared limits?
:::

We often forget that a tool command is not an environment. We can launch a simulator, compiler, formal engine, or physical-design flow, yet still struggle to identify which candidate actually ran, what hidden state the tool inherited, what an obscure warning meant, or whether a simple retry blindly repeated the exact same work. When we introduce AI-assisted methods, this operational gap becomes impossible to ignore, simply because these agents can fire off requests far faster than we can manually inspect the surrounding state for each invocation.

Suppose we want to evaluate a heterogeneous XR SoC, balancing matrix-multiply NPU execution throughput against LPDDR5 memory controller traffic, L2 cache capacity, and gate-level physical synthesis constraints. To screen candidate configurations, a quick analytical or SRAM evaluation screens candidates before we send the survivors into tightly budgeted rounds of cycle-level simulations, formal property checks, and place-and-route runs. For this to work, our tools must reliably return physical estimates, matched workload results, warnings, run failures, and the actual resources spent. If a run loses track of a candidate's identity or mismatches our test conditions, it might hand us perfectly plausible numbers for the completely wrong comparison. Worse, if a tool silently retries without limits, we could quickly blow past our declared study budget.

Even if our initial request clearly identifies which tools to use, it is rarely ready to execute as-is. We have to translate each conceptual candidate into the exact configuration format our tool expects. The workload, software stack, shared libraries, process assumptions, and specific tool versions all need to travel alongside that configuration. We also know that long-running jobs will sit in queues and wait for licenses. Tools will inevitably crash, time out, mysteriously drop reports, or even falsely report success after running the wrong top-level design entirely. When the dust settles, our returned files might trickle back hours later and completely out of order.

This is exactly why we build an enclosing environment to handle these messy mechanics. A robust environment proves that our requested work hit the specified tool in a known, named state, and it meticulously records what that attempt produced. However, the environment does not guarantee that the resulting metric is scientifically valid, nor does it tell us if the candidate is actually good. We must maintain this crucial distinction. Executing a well-formed run is not the same as supporting an architectural claim. To interpret the data and judge the claim itself, we need targeted checks that sit well outside the environment's responsibilities.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we can.

- Distinguish tools and simulators from their wrappers, harnesses, and enclosing environments.
- Pin environment state across hardware, software, and tools to guarantee reproducible execution.
- Design typed tool interfaces that precisely translate intent and return structured artifacts.
- Coordinate multi-tool asynchronous workflows within strict resource and permission boundaries.
- Separate execution failures from design-limit violations while preserving lineage.
:::

## Tool Environments

How do we decompose execution environments to isolate tool invocation, environment containment, and result extraction? We rarely find a single, monolithic component capable of carrying our request from a represented design state all the way to an identifiable tool return. To keep our pipelines manageable, we separate the responsibilities along this path into five distinct roles.

- A *tool* transforms an artifact or analyzes a stated property under our declared inputs and conditions. We consider compilers (such as LLVM and TVM), SRAM models, simulators (such as gem5, Verilator, and Synopsys VCS), RTL testbenches (such as Cocotb), formal property engines (using SystemVerilog Assertions and Bounded Model Checking, SVA/BMC), synthesis tools (such as Yosys and Xilinx Vivado), and place-and-route flows (such as OpenROAD) to be tools.
- A *simulator* is just one kind of tool. It executes a model of hardware and software behavior, returning only the behavior its model exposes. It never serves as the complete environment.
- A *wrapper* surrounds a single tool. It validates our request, translates that request into tool-specific inputs, invokes the tool, and parses the returned files.
- A *harness* coordinates our wrappers. It records our attempts, state, costs, failures, retries, resets, and produced artifacts.
- The *environment* is everything connecting our study to its underlying tools. It defines the state our method may observe, the requests we may issue, the tools we can reach, and the returns we expect to receive.

For example, we might build an XR SoC design environment containing wrappers for an SRAM model, a gem5 cycle-level CPU and NoC timing simulator, a Verilator C++ or Cocotb Python RTL model for an NPU systolic array, an SVA/BMC formal model checker for memory bus deadlock verification, a Yosys and Vivado synthesis tool, an OpenROAD physical signoff flow, enterprise ASIC hardware emulators (such as Synopsys ZeBu and Cadence Palladium), and a FireSim FPGA-accelerated target simulator. We then rely on one harness to keep their collective outputs, from NPU MAC utilization and memory traffic latency down to placed-and-routed timing slack, tied to the same candidate and experimental conditions.

We make this distinction because it is structural, not cosmetic. A simulator remains just a tool even if we give it a convenient Python interface, and a wrapper still serves only one tool at a time. While our harness can certainly coordinate several wrappers, it only becomes part of an environment when we use it to inspect relevant state, issue bounded requests, and receive identifiable returns.

We must ensure each request survives its full journey from a known starting state to an identifiable return. During setup, we establish our design, software, workload, tool, and resource state. Our interfaces and wrappers define exactly what we can request and translate it precisely. The runtime and harness then schedule, isolate, budget, cancel, retry, and record our work. Finally, our return includes the execution status, artifacts, parsed results, warnings, cost, and lineage. We maintain these responsibilities regardless of whether an architect, a conventional search, or a learned method issues the request.

While our broader design workflow certainly uses the environment, it does not belong to it. We use the workflow to direct the ordering of design tasks, method decisions, interpretation of returned results, and human review. The environment merely executes our authorized requests and exposes identifiable returns back to that overarching workflow.

Before submitting work, we must be able to inspect the candidate, fixed state, supported tool operations, resources, and prior attempts. The environment then accepts only our declared requests, returning the execution status, raw artifacts, parsed values, unclassified text, cost, and lineage. We keep request checking, tool execution, parsing, and run recording entirely separate throughout this path (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

![**A tool interface separates execution state from interpretation.** Our wrapper validates and translates the request, our tool executes the declared operation, our parser interprets retained output, and our harness records both the runtime outcome and the parse status.](images/F6-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface fig-alt="An architecture question and workload, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter our tool-connected environment as a typed request. Our wrapper validates and translates the request before calling the tool. An invalid request goes directly to our harness record. The tool separately produces raw returned material and a runtime outcome that can be failed, partial, or complete. Our parser turns retained raw material into structured attributes, unclassified residual output, and a parse status. Our harness records request and attempt identity, conditions, runtime outcome, artifacts, parse status, cost, and lineage."}

Our represented question and state enter the interface as a typed request. Our wrapper either refuses an invalid request immediately or translates it smoothly to the declared tool path. A valid invocation produces raw returned material alongside a runtime outcome. We use the parser to keep recognized properties, residual output, and its own interpretation status, while our harness records those extracted elements alongside the execution outcome, identity, cost, and lineage. Because we maintain this separation, a parser failure does not rewrite a complete tool invocation as a tool failure, and conversely, a clean parse cannot trick us into turning a partial tool return into a complete one.

Building this kind of robust environment challenges us precisely because our architecture tools often inherit state that our request never explicitly names, and they routinely return more material than we originally asked for.

## Stateful Tools and Partial Returns

How do tool harnesses encapsulate stateful EDA databases, partial executions, and non-deterministic environment returns? We cannot treat architecture tools like interchangeable, stateless services. Instead, we have to navigate a world where tools operate on massive, versioned artifacts and stash hidden state across working directories and databases. We wrestle with incompatible formats and units, wait in queues for shared machines and licenses, and often walk away with only partial files when long-running jobs fail. To evaluate a single candidate, our flow might string together software construction, functional simulation, register-transfer-level (RTL) models, formal checks, synthesis, and physical implementation. No generic software sandbox is going to automatically supply these hardware-specific semantics for us.

Take OpenROAD or Xilinx Vivado, for example, which expose stateful Tcl interfaces over complex design databases [@OpenROADDocs]. Similarly, commercial simulators like Synopsys VCS and formal engines using SystemVerilog Assertions and Bounded Model Checking (SVA/BMC) maintain persistent compilation state and intermediate coverage databases. When we build a wrapper for such a tool, we must establish or validate the declared state before every single invocation. We need to hook into the tool's error mechanism to return an explicit status and carefully serialize the recognized parameters. Crucially, we must also retain the raw transcript and any unclassified output. While a clean, structured record is undeniably useful, it simply isn't enough if we accidentally discard an unfamiliar warning during the parsing process.

In our real-world projects, we also inherit intellectual property (IP) blocks, NPU compiler toolchains, software stacks, constraints, generated files, vendor models, and tool databases. While our environment doesn't need to expose protected contents beyond what a specific study authorizes, we absolutely must preserve the exact identity, version, permitted use, and dependent state carried into each invocation. If we fail to track these details, a repeated request might look identical on the surface while secretly running against a completely different design or model underneath.

A typical implementation flow illustrates this problem perfectly. OpenROAD provides `read_liberty` for loading *Liberty library views* (`.lib` files containing characterized cell delays, setup/hold constraints, and power specifications) and `read_lef` for loading Library Exchange Format (LEF) technology and macro physical layout data [@OpenROADDocs], while Yosys ingests cell libraries for logic gate mapping. In an XR SoC design, an NPU accelerator block, LPDDR5 memory controller, or SRAM macro might appear as a behavioral C++/RTL model in Verilator, a Liberty timing and power view during Yosys or Vivado synthesis, and a LEF physical view during OpenROAD placement and routing. If we update the behavioral RTL model but accidentally retain an un-updated, *stale Liberty library view* from a previous cache, we allow different stages of our toolchain to evaluate conflicting physical and timing versions of what we treat as a single macro. This mismatch can produce deceptively clean signoff reports for designs that will physically fail on silicon. To prevent this, our environment must bind compatible views to a single identity, or outright refuse to run.

We must insist that translation is exact; otherwise, it must be refused. If our study asks for `l2.capacity=3MiB`, `npu.mesh=16x16`, or `mem.channels=2`, our wrapper might serialize those values into SRAM configuration files, compiler flags, and simulator parameters. However, we cannot let the wrapper silently round a cache capacity to the nearest power of two, shrink NPU mesh dimensions to force a legal floorplan, or quietly substitute another simulator just because it happens to be idle. Every one of those sneaky choices fundamentally changes the meaning of our request. While we can use a syntax-preserving repair to create a new request artifact or execution attempt (retaining the candidate identity), our wrapper must refuse any repair that alters architectural meaning. Instead, it should return a validation failure straight back to the candidate-producing caller. From there, the caller can leverage the enclosing lifecycle to generate a fresh candidate. We only reopen method selection if the failure completely invalidates our chosen approach or its supported action space.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One XR SoC request, several exact translations"}
Our 3\ MiB cache, $16 \times 16$ NPU array, and dual LPDDR5 memory channel candidate becomes a single SRAM and NPU analytical model input under our declared process, voltage, and temperature conditions. If our predeclared routing conditions permit, it also becomes a gem5 and Verilator simulation configuration linked to our specific NPU model, memory traffic generators, XR workload trace, and baseline software image. While our wrapper has the freedom to adjust file syntax, paths, and command-line spelling, we strictly forbid it from changing the cache policy, NPU systolic topology, memory controller arbitration, compiler runtime, workload, or any other architectural property. If the translation remains exact, we proceed. Anything else we immediately refuse and record.
:::

Enforcing this narrow rule, we prevent a frustratingly common failure mode. Often, an automated repair will make a tool call legal by silently altering the very design we set out to evaluate. The tool then runs cleanly and reports success, but we end up with results that belong to an entirely different candidate. Our request validation steps should catch these mismatches before we burn any expensive cluster time. Naturally, to perform this exact validation, we first need an unambiguously identifiable starting state.

## Setup and Lineage

How do pinned environment specifications and lineage tracking guarantee reproducible execution across shifting toolchains? Every requested run must begin from a known state. Before we start our first tool, we must pin, or intentionally mark as variable, all source and generated artifacts, workload inputs, tool and library versions, process design kit (PDK) views, constraints, environment variables, host resources, and baseline artifacts. Our run specification cements the relationship between this starting state, the represented request, the tool path, and the final returned artifacts. In short, it defines exactly how our requested work will execute without inadvertently altering the architectural comparison.

We define *lineage* as the parent-child history linking our requests, transformations, and artifacts. This history allows another architect to confidently trace which inputs produced a given result, and to verify whether a subsequent retry, software image, or hardware artifact actually belongs to the same candidate design.

While pinned state is necessary, it is not sufficient on its own. A simple retry might duplicate billable work, a crashed process could easily contaminate our next attempt, a flawed reset might restore an incorrect baseline, and improperly reused output can bleed across candidate or condition boundaries. Therefore, we need rigorous rules for failure, retry, reset, containment, and retention to prevent runtime behaviors from quietly altering our request's meaning or skyrocketing its realized cost. We gather these responsibilities into a single concrete example with the prospective cache-study run specification shown in @tbl-environment-contract.

We treat the versioned source, workload snapshots, constraints, libraries, PDK views, tool images, and baseline artifacts that kick off a run as immutable inputs. In contrast, our mutable work state encompasses the run directory, generated files, tool databases, checkpoints, scheduler state, and any other artifacts our requested action might alter. Our evaluation harness never patches immutable inputs in place; instead, it generates a fresh working state tied to those inputs and carefully logs every authorized mutation.

When we talk about a reset, we mean fully restoring a declared starting state, not merely invoking a function called `reset`. A clean reset completely regenerates our working directory and tool state from pinned inputs, whereas a checkpoint reset resumes from a verified intermediate database as long as its parent inputs and validity conditions remain identical. Before we consume scarce execution cycles, our setup checks must proactively confirm the expected top level, clocks, constraints, libraries, workload, tool version, and artifact set.

Our architecture tools rarely directly consume the high-level representation we used to formulate a study. For instance, an SRAM model requires a detailed organization and technology configuration, while a gem5 or Verilator simulator expects a platform description, an NPU binary image, and specific microarchitecture and memory bus parameters. Similarly, a power model might ingest activity and event counts produced by an entirely different tool. Our environment must seamlessly lower a single candidate into these varied formats while strictly preserving its parent relationship.

To track these complex identities and outcomes, we maintain a complete transformation record that captures.

- the parent candidate and request;
- the transformation and tool version;
- input identifiers and content hashes, where useful;
- fixed conditions inherited from our broader study;
- the output artifact alongside its hash;
- whether the transformation successfully preserved our intended architecture meaning; and
- the next authorized consumer.

When our serialization only modifies syntax, we retain the original candidate identity. This distinction becomes critical when our wrapper steps in to repair a malformed file. For example, adding a missing quote around `3MiB` clearly preserves the original meaning, but shrinking an NPU array dimension merely to appease a rigid parser completely breaks it.

While content hashes allow us to cleanly distinguish exact artifacts, they do not inherently prove that two artifacts are functionally equivalent or represent the same underlying architecture. We look to build systems like Bazel as strong examples of using declared dependencies and cached actions to enforce consistency [@Bazel2026Dependencies; @Bazel2026RemoteCaching]. Yet even with such rigorous discipline, hidden tool state can still sabotage our reproducibility, which is why our harness meticulously records both the final hash and the exact execution conditions.

Random seeds are just one form of variation control. Our setup must also pin thread counts, scheduler placement, parallel reduction order, host libraries, and, where our tools permit, the timing of concurrent jobs. If a tool's documentation points out a nondeterministic algorithm or heuristic, we must apply additional controls to tame it. In cases where we simply cannot fix a specific factor, our execution record must explicitly state what varied, retaining enough repeated attempts so we can statistically characterize repeatability later. Ultimately, we can study declared variation, but unrecorded variation acts as a hidden, toxic dependency.

When we introduce larger hardware and software changes, the full scope of the lineage problem becomes glaringly visible (as shown in @fig-artifact-lineage). A single root intent might branch out to produce an array of different software binaries and RTL artifacts.

![**Every evaluated artifact needs an identifiable parent.** Software and hardware artifacts derived from our proposals must retain their transformation history, and when we change an input, we create a new evaluation identity.](images/F5-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage fig-alt="Our single Lighthouse intent branches into a software variant and a hardware variant. The software compiles into an identified binary, and the hardware elaborates into an identified RTL artifact. Our evaluation instance binds both artifacts to the tool and version, workload, and operating conditions. Hashes and evaluation keys distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

In our displayed branch, the Lighthouse intent yields one software variant and one hardware variant. The software variant compiles down into an identified binary, while the hardware elaborates into a specific RTL artifact. We then combine this selected pair to form a single evaluation instance. If we replace either child component, we generate an entirely different pair, even if our root intent remains untouched. While our artifact hashes distinguish the exact files and their transformation paths, the evaluation key takes this a step further by binding the pair to the specific tool, version, workload, and operating conditions. Unfortunately, even these stringent identities fail to guarantee functional equivalence or true reproducibility if we leave relevant state undeclared.

Hidden or mismatched conditions can invalidate an identity match just as quickly as a stale artifact. When we receive an SRAM-model return, it carries deep circuit and technology assumptions strictly bound to its declared process, voltage, and temperature settings. Likewise, an OpenROAD or Vivado implementation return is permanently tethered to its specific corner, mode, libraries, constraints, and flags. The returns we pull from cycle-level simulation, cache models, and power models carry equally heavy baggage, including workload, software, warm-up length, measured region, seed, checkpoint, and model configuration. Our environment must retain all conditions that apply to each tool, safely marking any nonapplicable parameters without independently judging if those conditions are sufficient. A timing-slack return of $-12\,\mathrm{ps}$ at a slow process corner is fundamentally not interchangeable with the exact same numeric return taken at a typical corner. The number itself must travel seamlessly with the conditions that give it meaning.

We must also recognize that our host environment itself can warp a result. As Mytkowicz and colleagues demonstrated, something as mundane as link order or UNIX environment size can perturb measured performance by a margin larger than many highly touted optimizations [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. If we give an optimizer enough attempts, it will inevitably exploit these shadowy effects. By rigorously pinning and recording the binary, host, environment variables, and flags, we prevent accidental host discrepancies from masquerading as genuine candidate improvements.

While our pinned state firmly establishes the foundation from which a run begins, our task does not end there. Our wrapper must now expose the specific changes a method is allowed to request, doing so without accidentally erasing the critical meaning behind the tool-specific return.

## Typed Interfaces

How do typed request and return schemas enforce interface contracts across heterogeneous EDA and simulation tools? We use wrappers to transform a known starting state into a single, focused tool interface. When we define a request schema, we explicitly name every parameter, type, unit, required input, default value, and legal combination. Similarly, our return schema specifies every structured attribute, unit, status code, warning class, and raw artifact. For example, if we have an NPU buffer capacity attribute measured in bytes, it must reject an unqualified `3`; likewise, our timing results cannot leave us guessing whether the unit represents CPU cycles, nanoseconds, or simulator ticks.

To build a truly usable interface across a heterogeneous XR SoC design flow, we construct dedicated wrappers tailored to specific tool paradigms. We wrap cycle-level simulators (gem5) to extract IPC and contention metrics [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5]. We wrap RTL simulators (Verilator, VCS) and Python verification harnesses (Cocotb) to compile models and parse waveform traces or timing violations [@Veripool2026Verilator]. We wrap formal engines (SVA/BMC) to serialize invariants and return proof certificates [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. For implementation, we wrap synthesis and physical design flows (Yosys, Vivado, OpenROAD) to translate constraints into stateful Tcl executions and parse slack and power signoffs [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD; @OpenROADDocs]. Finally, we wrap enterprise ASIC hardware emulators (Synopsys ZeBu, Cadence Palladium) and FPGA-accelerated simulators (FireSim) to manage hardware targets and parse high-throughput traces [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim].

To build a usable interface, we must clearly distinguish the underlying state from what the caller actually observes. We consider *state* to be the relevant condition of our design, software, tools, runtime, resources, and outstanding work. An *observation*, on the other hand, represents the authorized portion of that state, or a returned result, that we choose to expose to the caller. We define an *action* as a permitted, typed request complete with its own identity and preconditions, while a *transition* records exactly what changed when we accepted, completed, failed, canceled, or reset that action. Ultimately, a tool *return* combines the raw and structured output of a single attempt alongside its execution status. As we discuss in @sec-feedback-verification-trust, we must evaluate whether any returned property can reliably support our measurement, update, or stopping decisions.

Our interface must also clearly define which project state the caller can read and which parameters it can change. For instance, an NPU-sizing wrapper might let us modify array dimensions and local memory buffer capacity while keeping interconnect topology, compiler flags, and memory traffic profiles strictly read-only. We ensure the wrapper outright refuses any request falling outside this permitted action set, rather than silently projecting our request onto the nearest supported design.

Standardizing attributes across our tooling, we eliminate accidental interface differences without obscuring the tool's core meaning. When we share the same request identity, allowed actions, job status, errors, cost, cancellation, retry, and lineage tracking, multiple methods can leverage a single tool path under unified action and budget rules. This consistency also allows our methods to move seamlessly among compatible tool paths without forcing us to reimplement scheduling and failure handling. While the resulting request and execution records become directly comparable across our methods, the actual measurements, candidate quality, and conclusions naturally remain distinct. We can only replace a wrapper or tool path when its declared capabilities, properties, conditions, schemas, and semantics align. Even then, we require each wrapper to transparently expose its supported operations, stages, properties, fidelities, units, assumptions, defaults, and warnings.

Capability and schema discovery make this separation fully inspectable. We ensure each request and return explicitly records the versions of the wrapper, request-schema, return-schema, parser, and underlying tool. This allows our callers to inspect supported actions and parameters before submitting any work. If a request is unsupported, our interface refuses it outright rather than silently dropping an argument, changing a default, or substituting a different fidelity. Furthermore, we never reinterpret a retained request under a newer schema; instead, we handle explicit migrations by creating a brand-new request artifact that links back to the original.

We must treat errors as a first-class part of our interface. Validation errors, tool diagnostics, missing outputs, parse failures, and unclassified warnings must remain distinct and retain their original text. While a typed result makes routine values much easier to consume, our wrapper cannot simply discard output just because the current schema fails to recognize it. Keeping raw output, parsed attributes, execution outcomes, and run identity on strictly separate paths, we prevent one component from silently assigning meaning to another component's result (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

Our environment does not necessarily need to return a single scalar reward. We might design a method that later derives an objective or reward from the returned values, but this derived value must remain separate from our raw observations and can never replace them. Consequently, a shared interface standardizes how we request and return work, intentionally leaving our architecture objectives and nuanced interpretations outside the wrapper itself.

When structured hardware representations match the underlying artifact, they can significantly reduce ambiguity. For example, Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) provides documented hardware dialects and compiler passes that let us operate directly on structured intermediate representations, sparing us from treating every change as a fragile textual source edit [@CIRCT]. However, we view this as a highly useful interface technique rather than the definition of an environment. We must remember that sharing a CIRCT operation, a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schema, or a simulator request does not magically make two tools equal in fidelity. Ultimately, our chosen tool model, setup, and returned properties still dictate exactly what each observation contains.

Before we introduce a wrapper into a study, we should rigorously test its translation and control paths using known fixtures. We design each fixture to pair a typed request with its expected command line, translated inputs, retained artifacts, and parsed return. Our legal test cases must match the values reported by tool introspection or those preserved in the translated input, just as our illegal requests must be decisively refused. Enforcing these checks, we can catch silent defaults, unexpected unit conversions, stale working state, and parsers that mistakenly accept output from the wrong run.

We also use failure injection to exercise the error-handling mechanics that our routine runs seldom reach. Our test harness can force a timeout, kill a process, omit or truncate output, and intentionally leave stale state, allowing us to verify our cancellation, retry, reset, and parsing behaviors. We must rerun these tests whenever our wrapper, parser, schema, library, or tool version changes. We keep in mind that passing tests only prove that our translation, control, state management, and parsing behave as declared for those specific requests, faults, states, and tool versions; any untested combinations remain a complete unknown.

Cloud systems offer us a valuable precedent here. Frameworks like FATE and DESTINI inject faults to exercise recovery paths and verify whether the resulting behavior matches a formally declared recovery policy [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini]. While we can easily adopt this testing philosophy for an EDA wrapper, we must recognize that borrowing from the cloud community does not automatically prove our wrapper preserves architecture meaning, covers tool-specific failure modes, or guarantees that a recovery retry is safe. To confidently make those claims, we still need purpose-built fixtures and fault injections tied directly to our actual tool paths.

Once a request successfully crosses our tested interface, the runtime must keep the request's identity perfectly intact while the work waits, runs, fails, or returns.

## Managing Asynchronous Runs

How do scheduler adapters manage asynchronous tool execution, license queuing, and checkpointing across distributed clusters? Architecture work rarely fits neatly into a single blocking function call. Instead, our cycle simulations might run for hours. Our physical-design jobs often sit in queues waiting for scarce licenses, produce massive intermediate databases, or fail after grinding through substantial work. We see tool state persist across working directories, caches, checkpoints, license servers, random seeds, and generated artifacts, while the outputs themselves often return asynchronously or out of order. Furthermore, we frequently find that one tool path depends directly on an artifact produced by another.

A familiar reinforcement-learning environment presents a synchronous `step()` interface that returns an observation, reward, termination flags, and auxiliary information [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium]. We generally cannot reduce architecture execution to such a simple exchange. Our runtime has to preserve the complex queueing, dependency, persistent state, and ordering behaviors we just described, along with the typed tool returns. When we actually need a reward, our methods can derive one afterward from this rich execution data.

We connect our harness to a scheduler or execution backend using a *scheduler adapter*. This adapter maps our stable harness operations, like submitting a job, inspecting its status, and canceling it, onto a specific backend (such as Slurm, IBM Spectrum LSF, or cloud container schedulers). However, it does not replace our tool wrappers; we still rely on those wrappers to own the tool-specific validation, translation, invocation, and parsing.

At a minimum, we require that a caller can inspect backend capabilities and state, submit a typed request, receive an attempt identifier, inspect or cancel that attempt, and ultimately receive its raw and parsed returns, status, warnings, cost, and lineage. We might see a single request produce no backend job, one job, or even several jobs or execution segments. All these cases still belong to a single attempt, and we ensure that attempt retains separate properties detailing how the work was scheduled, why it ended, what artifacts exist, what our parser recognized, whether cancellation completed, and which prior attempt authorized a retry. We illustrate these object relationships in @fig-runtime-object-state.

![**One attempt can contain zero, one, or several backend executions.** Our attempt record keeps backend work securely attached to the authorized request while preserving returned artifacts, our realized cost, and independent status properties.](images/F6c-runtime-object-state){#fig-runtime-object-state fig-alt="An authorized request creates one attempt. The attempt may be refused before a backend job exists, may create one job, or may create several jobs or execution segments. All paths feed one attempt record. The attempt record points separately to returned artifacts and realized cost. Scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, cancellation confirmation, and retry parent remain independent attributes."}

The figure separates object identity from state classification. For example, if we submit a request that fails admission, we still generate an attempt record even though no scheduler job exists. Similarly, our multi-stage physical-design invocations might create several backend segments without becoming multiple candidates. We ensure returned artifacts and realized costs remain firmly attached to the attempt, even for work that failed, was canceled, or was retried. Keeping the six status indicators independent, we prevent a terminal process state from falsely implying that we have complete artifacts, a successful parse, or a confirmed cancellation.

### Tracking Attempts and Jobs

When we make a request, we specify an allowed action for a candidate under declared conditions. We define each authorized try as an attempt. Every job and segment we spawn retains that attempt identifier. If our study requires an intentional repeat, we treat it as a planned new attempt; in contrast, a recovery retry is a new attempt we authorize because our prior execution failed or returned incompletely. We develop the detailed retry policy in the Recovery section later in this chapter.

Our harness attaches every job or segment to its attempt right at submission, well before a late result could possibly arrive. We keep our dependencies perfectly explicit. For instance, our compiler builds might wait for a source artifact, our RTL simulations in Verilator or VCS might wait for elaboration, and our physical implementations in OpenROAD or Vivado might wait for a mapped netlist from Yosys. We can run independent jobs concurrently, but we never let that concurrency relax their strict identity or resource limits.

Because the scheduler might accept work before our harness records the job identifier, we explicitly tag our submitted work with the attempt identifier and reconcile our records with the scheduler before ever resubmitting. We rely on an *idempotency key*, a unique request identifier whose durable backend handling prevents a repeated submission from accidentally launching the same work twice. In our system, `submission_token` serves exactly this role. The backend records this key alongside the first admission result, ensuring that any later submission bearing the same key simply identifies the existing attempt or job. We design our harness to retain this key throughout the retry window, reconcile it cleanly after a crash, and outright reject its reuse for any different request [@Featonby2021IdempotentAPIs].

We know all too well that a backend status of `running` does not establish useful progress. Whenever the tool or backend exposes them, our harness retains advisory metrics, such as the last heartbeat or output time, the current tool stage or checkpoint, and any resources or licenses still held. We can use these indicators to support escalation or cancellation decisions, but we never let them prove architecture progress or validate a returned result.

### Scoping Budgets and Preemption

When we design our authorization, we strictly follow the established security principle of least privilege [@SaltzerSchroeder1975ProtectionInformation]. We ensure a wrapper receives only the executables, filesystem paths, network destinations, credentials, secrets, licensed features, and intellectual property absolutely needed for its declared action. We treat generated scripts, constraints, RTL, and compiler inputs as completely untrusted until we validate and confine them. Consequently, we isolate every single attempt within its own dedicated working area, strict resource limits, and strong process boundaries. If we fail to do this, a malformed RTL candidate might easily corrupt a shared worktree, fill a disk, exhaust host memory, or completely wedge a license process. Enforcing isolation, our harness safely traps failures and returns control without mistakenly treating the candidate as fully measured.

We apply this exact same confinement to the material we supply to our models, just as we do for our tool processes. Our projects operate in segregated workspaces, with isolated retrieval indexes, caches, checkpoints, model contexts, logs, and credentials. We tightly scope each resource to its specific project, permissions, confidentiality limits, and retention policies. For every request, our wrapper selects an authorized context set, permits only explicitly declared egress routes, and steadfastly refuses to send any material not authorized to cross the destination boundary. We only allow the reuse of caches or checkpoints across scopes when their identities and permissions perfectly match. While these robust controls drastically reduce accidental mixing and disclosure, we still require separate manual reviews for source permissions and generated-output provenance.

We apply budgets independently across our model calls, tool submissions, elapsed time, CPU and accelerator usage, memory, storage, and license occupancy. Our admission checks carefully reserve scarce resources before we ever dispatch a job. Of course, even an accepted request might still be queued, canceled, or fail entirely; similarly, a seemingly completed run might still be missing a critical artifact. We use these distinct states to determine exactly what our runtime records and which recovery actions remain available to us.

Our automated work inevitably shares queues, machines, storage, and software licenses with human engineers and massive production flows. When these shared resources inevitably saturate, our environment applies the site's in-flight limits, project quotas or priorities, reservations, and backpressure to intelligently slow down or outright refuse new work. We design the environment to expose pending work, accepted work, and remaining authorizations, ensuring our methods never blindly resubmit just because a queued job hasn't become visible yet.

We must remember that cancellation is not complete the moment we issue a stop request. Instead, our harness explicitly requests the termination of all descendants, and then rigidly confirms both process termination and license release. We know a process might stop after producing partial artifacts, or it might rush to completion before our cancellation even takes effect. We ensure any late return remains permanently attached to its original attempt, keeping it strictly out of our live state until the current request revision and our strict budget policies officially admit it.

We enforce a finite deadline for every attempt to confirm its terminal state. Our timeouts clearly state whether they bound a queue wait, a run time, a single tool stage, or serve as an absolute wall-clock deadline. If we find that scheduler and process states disagree, or remain entirely unknown past that deadline, our harness retains the attempt as unconfirmed, instantly quarantines the uncertain outputs, and rigorously prevents any late writers from mutating our live state. Crucially, we preserve enough of the partial state to explain exactly what happened. Ultimately, this explicit confirmation step is how we transform a chaotic cancellation request or timeout into a tightly controlled runtime outcome.

### Recording Execution Costs

We built our execution interface to keep every request identifiable as it moves through validation, admission, scheduling, termination, artifact inspection, and parsing. In our common case, a single attempt produces one scheduler job, but our records deliberately keep those stages and their outcomes completely distinct.

Our records must answer precisely what we requested, what actually ran, how it ended, and what it cost us. We use the request and the run specification to define our authorized work. We then rely on our attempt, job, and segment identifiers to show us exactly what reached a backend. Our attempt record joins all these objects to the returned material and our realized cost. Keeping these concepts separate prevents a simple retry from spawning a new candidate, or an intermediate scheduler job from masquerading as a final architecture result.

We use `candidate_id` to uniquely name our architecture candidate across all tool paths. Similarly, we use `configuration_id` to name that candidate's declared tool-specific configuration record for the requested path, rather than naming the translated files themselves. Once we validate those translated files, we assign them separate artifact identifiers and hashes. We retain both identities because a single candidate might require several tool-specific configurations, while we might also execute several attempts using the exact same candidate and configuration.

Before submission, our harness meticulously retains the request, the authorized attempt, and all translated inputs. If we hit an invalid translation, an unmet setup dependency, an exhausted budget, or a refused admission, we simply produce an attempt record with no scheduler job rather than letting the failure quietly disappear from our records. Once the backend accepts the work, we link the job to the attempt through its entire lifecycle, while it is queued, running, and terminal. Of course, a terminal process still requires us to perform full artifact inspection and parsing.

After the process stops, we ensure the very same attempt record retains the terminal cause, our expected-artifact check, the parser status, the raw and structured output, any retry eligibility, resource use, cost, and full lineage. Keeping these attributes distinctly separate lets our runtime easily distinguish a disastrous tool crash from a merely missing report or an outdated parser.

We record our resources separately instead of lazily collapsing them into a single cost value. Our harness preserves tool and candidate identity alongside submission, queue, start, completion, and elapsed times. We also carefully track our central processing unit (CPU) and accelerator usage, peak memory and storage, license occupancy, model and tool calls, retries and cancellations, and any linked setup, diagnosis, review, and repair work.

For our scheduler-managed resources, our records distinguish between reserved, consumed, and billable amounts whenever they are available; we explicitly give their units, and we name the specific scheduler, license server, or billing system that supplied each value. We leave any variables that our environment cannot directly observe explicitly unreported. Furthermore, we allow human work to attach to a group of attempts whenever a single setup or diagnosis effort supports several invocations.

The decisive distinction we draw is between one identified candidate-configuration pair and the many attempts we might use to execute it. When we retry the same pair, we increase our realized cost, but we do not create another candidate, a new tool-specific configuration, or a fully independent observation. The setup and cost we record must travel alongside any returned value that later becomes data. Enforcing this, we ensure that a later study can accurately compare time, compute, storage, and license use without absurdly treating a cycle simulation, a physical-design run, and a simple model call as equivalent samples.

Before we ever choose a retry, a reset, a checkpoint, or a cached artifact, our harness must first meticulously determine exactly what the attempt returned. Our runtime establishes what actually ran, what returned, and what our work cost. However, it never assumes that a returned value is inherently valid or that our candidate should automatically advance.

## Failure Classification

How does structured failure classification distinguish execution failures from architectural candidate rejections? When we run tools, they fail in a variety of ways, and we cannot adequately represent these outcomes with a single `FAILED` value. We must separate the terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and retry eligibility into distinct attributes. The rows below highlight common combinations rather than forcing everything into one exclusive status value. Because these attributes dictate what our harness repairs and what it hands forward, they strictly describe execution rather than rendering an architecture judgment (@tbl-failure-taxonomy).

When we incorporate formal tools, maintaining this separation becomes especially critical. Model-checking variants often report different outcomes and attach unique assumptions, bounds, or artifacts [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. Rather than translating every completed formal run into one generic status, our environment preserves the exact terminology reported by each specific formal method and tool, including theorem provers and equivalence checkers.

| **Execution outcome** | **How it appears** | **What our harness preserves** | **Our runtime response** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Invalid request** | We find an illegal value, missing identity, or meaning-changing translation before invocation. | Request, validation rule, and refusal reason. | We repair syntax only when meaning is preserved; otherwise, we refuse the request and return it to the candidate-producing caller. We reopen method selection only if the failure invalidates our chosen approach or its supported action space. |
| **Setup or dependency failure** | We detect that the top level, clock, library, constraint, checkpoint, or generated input is missing or stale. | Setup check, diagnostics, partial artifacts, and realized cost. | We restore or regenerate the declared state, leaving the candidate unevaluated. |
| **Infrastructure failure** | We find a license, host, scheduler, or storage service unavailable. | Attempt, failure source, partial artifacts, cost, and retry eligibility. | We retry only under the declared policy, leaving the candidate unevaluated. |
| **Tool failure** | The tool crashes (such as a Vivado routing error, gem5 out-of-memory exception, or VCS elaboration failure), reports an internal error, or exhausts a local resource. | Tool status, diagnostics, partial artifacts, conditions, cost, and retry history. | We retry, reset, resume a valid checkpoint, or stop entirely. We recognize that repetition does not prove physical infeasibility. |
| **Incomplete return** | We notice a stage or expected report is missing, stale, or only partly written. | Completed stages, expected-artifact check, produced files, raw output, and parse status. | We preserve the partial return and repair or rerun before treating it as complete. |
| **Parser failure** | A retained artifact does not match our declared schema or contains unclassified output. | Parser version, raw artifact, diagnostics, recognized elements, and residual output. | We repair the parser and reparse the retained artifact when it is safe to do so. |
| **Formal-tool return** | The declared method and tool (such as an SVA/BMC checker) report their exact outcome, which may include a proof, counterexample VCD trace, bounded result, `unknown`, or resource limit. | Method, property or relation, model, assumptions, bound where applicable, tool, exact outcome, artifact, and cost. | We hand the method-specific result forward without turning it into a general correctness verdict. |
| **Reported design-limit violation** | A completed run reports a timing (such as OpenROAD WNS $< 0$), power, congestion, design-rule, or functional violation. | Typed violation, units, candidate, conditions, warnings, raw artifact, and cost. | We record a complete return without rejecting or penalizing the candidate. |
| **Complete tool return** | Our expected artifacts exist and parse successfully, including reports that contain violations. | Typed data, units, conditions, warnings, raw artifacts, cost, and lineage. | We retain the return for measurement qualification without deciding what it establishes. |

: **Our execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.** We keep invalid requests, failed paths, partial returns, parser failures, and complete returns separate so our subsequent repairs target the precise problem. {#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[18,25,31,26]"}

Our execution condition determines both the retained record and our next action. When we encounter invalid requests, setup failures, and infrastructure failures, we leave the candidate unevaluated. If we hit tool, artifact, or parser failures, we rely on different owners to repair them. Although a formal-tool return and a reported design-limit violation are completed returns rather than process failures, neither supplies us with a broad design verdict. We pass every completed result forward with its scope entirely intact.

We only consider a clean exit as a complete tool return after our expected-artifact check and parser succeed. Consider a synthesis script in Yosys or Vivado where we select no valid top-level module and omit the primary clock. Even though the process might exit with a status of zero and produce empty reports, our harness records a completed process alongside the missing artifacts and failed setup checks, rather than incorrectly substituting zeros for area, power, and timing.

Physical-design stages perfectly illustrate why a complete return may still contain a reported limit violation. Logic synthesis returns a mapped netlist, constraints, warnings, and early area and timing estimates, but lacks any placed or routed interconnect. As we move through the flow, floorplanning and placement add locations, utilization, congestion estimates, and a tool database. Finally, our clocking, routing, and power analysis stages contribute stage-specific timing, design-rule, congestion, and power results [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD; @OpenROADDocs]. We record exactly which stage produced each artifact, ensuring an early estimate cannot masquerade as a later report.

Our signoff returns remain strictly tied to the tool, libraries, corner, mode, constraints, warnings, and waivers that produced them. They never cover properties or conditions that we did not run. Consequently, even when we receive a complete signoff return, it supplies us with neither architecture interpretation nor authorization to proceed.

We always keep raw logs as part of the return. A commercial EDA tool or a detailed simulator may emit exceptionally long logs, and as we know, a language model can easily miss relevant text within a long context [@Liu2024LostInTheMiddle]. However, discarding everything outside a fixed parser is equally unsafe. Instead, our wrapper returns structured elements for recognized metrics and failures, an explicitly marked residual of unclassified warnings and errors, and both a retrievable artifact identifier and an integrity hash for the complete raw log.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The parser recognizes only yesterday's warnings"}
**The trap.** Our parser keeps only known warning classes and drops every line it cannot classify.

**The mechanism.** A new warning about a downgraded timing constraint or changed clock definition appears after we upgrade a tool. Because we never taught our parser the new class, it produces a dangerously clean, structured record.

**The lesson.** We must preserve unclassified warning and error lines alongside the raw log. Although a compact return should reduce our reading cost, it must not grant the parser permission to decide that unfamiliar output is irrelevant.
:::

We apply this same rule to partial returns. A placement density map produced just before a router crash may help our later diagnosis, but it remains a purely partial artifact. Our environment records exactly what stage produced it and what never ran. Later, during our measurement qualification, we determine whether that artifact actually bears on any claim.

Once we classify these outcomes, our harness can intelligently choose an allowed repair, retry, reset, checkpoint resume, cache reuse, or outright refusal, all without mistakenly treating a complete return as failed work.

## Recovery and Reuse

What rules govern safe artifact reuse, identity preservation, and recovery retries in automated tool pipelines? When we trigger a recovery retry, we launch a new attempt linked to the failed or incomplete one, rather than continuing and erasing what already happened. This differs from a planned repeat, where we request multiple runs independently of any failure. Our records must state exactly which inputs we reused, which state we reset, which checkpoint we resumed, and why we authorized another attempt. If we merely pause the scheduler and continue the same submitted job, it retains its original identity. However, when we authorize a restart from a checkpoint or perform a clean reset, we create a linked but distinct attempt. If a retry loses this lineage, our automated methods might easily mistake it for a brand new candidate, double-counting our evaluation evidence and rendering the sequence irreproducible. If we observe repeated failures under controlled conditions, we might expose a reproducible tool problem, but we have not necessarily proven that the design is physically infeasible.

How we handle recovery depends entirely on the class of failure. We repair invalid requests before a tool ever runs. If we encounter setup and parser defects, we usually require a clean restart once we fix the wrapper. Conversely, if we hit a transient host or license failure, we can often just retry the job. Eligibility for these retries hinges directly on the underlying cause. In our run specification, we assign recovery retries a declared maximum or budget. We then recheck admission requirements, ensuring that any clean restart or checkpoint resume relies strictly on compatible, explicitly identified state. If we find that an upgrade caused the failure, reverting to the last pinned version generates a new attempt rather than quietly rewriting the existing record.

We apply the same strict rules for identity and permissions to ensure safe caching. We can only reuse a complete return when its project scope, permissions, inputs, transformations, tools, libraries, PDK views, flags, conditions, and relevant state perfectly match the cache key. Even if a checkpoint or cache entry technically matches, we never let it cross into another project, confidentiality boundary, or license scope without explicit authorization. When we place a generator in the tool path, its context window becomes a critical part of that state. We must clear this window between evaluating an open-source baseline and analyzing proprietary work, just as we would refuse to reuse a cache entry across different scopes. While partial and failed outputs might help us diagnose issues, we never serve them as completed observations. Finally, if we detect any unknown dependencies, we immediately invalidate the cache entry.

Reusing cached timing or layout views across a design revision carries substantial operational risk.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Stale Liberty library views and silent signoff failures"}
**The claim.** An engineering team updated memory controller RTL and timing constraints for a 3.2\ GHz multi-die ASIC tapeout.

**The gap.** While the RTL and LEF layout views were updated for the new clock frequency, the static timing analysis (STA) flow inadvertently loaded an older Liberty (`.lib`) view from a cached 2.4\ GHz process corner. OpenSTA reported clean timing signoff because the stale Liberty file lacked setup/hold checks for the faster clock domain.

**The lesson.** Reusing stale library views or failing to flush cached tool workspace state can produce deceptively clean signoff reports for failing designs. When we design an architecture harness, we must validate PDK, LEF, and Liberty view checksums against candidate specifications before executing timing or physical signoff.
:::

This lesson extends far beyond a single accident. For our own systems, reuse remains safe only when we guarantee that the specific conditions making the prior execution meaningful still hold true today.


We keep all our recovery and reuse choices documented within the affected attempt record. Ultimately, our enclosing execution record ties the run specification and initial request to every linked attempt, artifact, return, and cost, ensuring we maintain a complete accounting of our work, even when it fails.

## Execution Records {#sec-operational-attempt-record}

How do operational attempt records capture tool state, cost metrics, and full execution provenance? Our returned records make the runtime object model concrete. Across these attempt records, we preserve exactly what we requested, attempted, returned, and spent. We retain raw logs, reports, traces, databases, and counterexamples to capture details that our current parsers might miss. At the same time, structured attributes make status, metrics, warnings, costs, and identity inspectable without forcing us to reread every file. We maintain both views in the execution record because neither perspective is sufficient on its own.

We treat this as a logical record rather than a mandate to build a new database. We can map these attributes and links directly onto our existing run directories, scheduler records, artifact stores, and review logs, provided we keep the attempt identities and their relationships recoverable. The enclosing record carries our study and request context, preserves the ordered attempt identifiers, and aggregates costs without hiding any repeated or retried work.

At a minimum, we require every attempt to capture these core elements.

- **Request and attempt identity:** We track the study, request, run specification, candidate, configuration, workload, software, conditions, and the unique attempt identifier.
- **Starting state:** We record the exact inputs, source revisions, artifact identities, and any behavior-affecting state and versions necessary to interpret or repeat the attempt.
- **Execution outcome:** We log whether the request was refused, or if the attempt failed, was canceled, returned partially, or completed. We also note the terminal cause, termination confirmation, artifact and parser status, and retry eligibility.
- **Returned material:** We retain raw artifacts and logs, hashes, structured values with their units, warnings, unclassified residual outputs, and measures of artifact completeness.
- **Lineage and retry relation:** We preserve parent inputs and artifacts, recorded transformations, and whether the attempt serves as an initial run, a planned repeat, or a recovery retry, alongside any retry or reset parent.
- **Realized cost:** We account for the amounts and units actually spent, capturing all failed, canceled, repeated, and retried work.

We can introduce tool-specific extensions to add meaning without altering the underlying attempt identity. For instance, an SVA/BMC formal run adds its properties, assumptions, bounds, solver outcomes, and any resulting proofs or counterexamples. An OpenROAD or Vivado physical-design run incorporates libraries, PDK views, modes, corners, constraints, waivers, stage databases, and stage statuses. A gem5 or Verilator sampled simulation includes its seed, region, warm-up period, checkpoints, thread count, and declared sources of variation. Furthermore, our resource services might attach queue and run times, compute usage, memory, storage, license occupancy, and any reserved, consumed, or billable amounts alongside their units and sources. Importantly, none of these extensions elevate a simple retry, stage, or resource report into a separate architecture result.

We must keep our unknowns explicit. If a value is unavailable or unobservable, we mark it as unreported or unknown; if a particular attribute simply does not apply, we indicate that separately. We never try to repair a missing seed, library view, or raw report by just leaving its entry blank. Ultimately, resource use represents just one part of the record, it never substitutes for a rigorous accounting of our starting state, status, lineage, or returned material.

What another architect can actually achieve with our records depends heavily on who repeats the work and the setup they use. The Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) distinguishes three related claims [@ACM2020ArtifactReview]. *Repeatability* means that our own team uses the same experimental setup to obtain the result again. *Replicability* means that a different team obtains the result using our original setup. *Reproducibility* means that a different team obtains the result using a completely different setup. In this chapter, we use *exact replay* as a narrower, book-specific term to describe submitting the identical retained request, artifacts, versions, and recorded state over again. A replay record simply shows that we requested the exact same retained inputs; it does not guarantee an identical realized execution or matching output bits. Across our architecture work, all four of these claims still require a shared agreement to interpret them meaningfully against the properties, variations, and operating conditions we are actively studying.

We can look to the Popper Convention for a strong systems precedent on placing experimental steps, parameters, and dependencies directly into a version-controlled, executable workflow [@JimenezEtAl2017PopperConvention]. While this practice certainly makes an architecture experiment much easier to inspect and rerun, it cannot by itself package licensed tools, proprietary process design kits, or protected design data. Furthermore, an executable workflow alone does not prove that two distinct tool paths preserve the same architectural meaning.

While hashes successfully establish the identity and integrity of exact bytes, they do not prove that two netlists are equivalent, that two configurations express the same architecture, or that two separate runs support a valid comparison. To establish those deeper relationships, we require the relevant transformation records and subsequent checks. We must maintain this crucial distinction even as a single candidate branches its way through several complex tools.

## Multi-Tool Toolchains

How do multi-fidelity toolchains coordinate heterogeneous evaluation tools while preserving cross-tool semantic validity? We often rely on multiple tools in our architecture studies because no single instrument can capture every relevant property. We can draw inspiration from multifidelity methods, which combine models of varying cost and accuracy for the specific quantity we want to measure [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. In this chapter, we apply that same principle to our architecture toolchains. We define *fidelity* not as a single scalar score, but as a measure of how faithfully a tool path represents a specific property under stated conditions. A path might offer high fidelity for one metric while remaining completely silent on another. For example, a FireSim FPGA-accelerated simulation lets us execute a target model much faster than an RTL simulation in Verilator, but it will not give us ASIC placement or OpenSTA timing signoff. Similarly, we can use a circuit model to estimate SRAM area and access time without ever executing the actual workload.

We organize these evaluation options along a *multi-fidelity spectrum*, establishing a structured continuum of tool execution paths ranging from fast analytical estimators to cycle-accurate simulators, emulator platforms, and physical signoff flows. This spectrum allows us to identify what each tool actually models and what our environment must retain to keep those results meaningful (@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum).

| **Tool class** | **Representative use** | **What it models or checks** | **What our environment must preserve** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical or circuit model | Spreadsheet, CACTI SRAM model, or NPU analytical energy estimator [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Encoded equations or circuit and technology assumptions, without workload execution. | Model version, organization, technology assumptions, units, and limits. |
| Compiler and software build | Target compiler (TVM, IREE, LLVM), lowering passes, assembler, linker, libraries, and runtime image. | Whether the declared source and mapping produce expected executable artifacts; no hardware timing or physical result. | Source and intermediate representations, target features, flags, mapping, library and compiler versions, diagnostics, and binary identity. |
| Functional instruction-set architecture (ISA) execution | Spike or QEMU ISA-level functional execution. | Instruction and software behavior under our implemented ISA model, without microarchitectural timing. | Binary, ISA options, input, termination state, and functional output. |
| Timing-model simulation | gem5 processor, NoC interconnect, and LPDDR5 memory controller timing simulation [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5]. | Modeled pipeline, cache, interconnect, and memory timing under a chosen configuration. | Workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, configuration, event counts, and traces. |
| RTL simulation and verification harness | Verilator C++ model execution [@Veripool2026Verilator], Cocotb Python testbenches, or Synopsys VCS gate-level simulation with SDF timing back-annotation. | Cycle behavior under our supplied RTL and simulator/testbench semantics; no routed-delay result unless we explicitly supply such timing. | RTL identity, testbench, compile flags, reset, waves, assertions, and logs. |
| Formal property or equivalence tool | SystemVerilog Assertions and Bounded Model Checking (SVA/BMC via SymbiYosys or JasperGold) [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. | The stated property or equivalence relation within our declared assumptions, abstraction, and bound where applicable; no general correctness result. | Property and model identities, assumptions, abstraction, bound, solver version and outcome, proof or counterexample artifact, and cost. |
| Enterprise emulation and FPGA acceleration | Synopsys ZeBu, Cadence Palladium enterprise emulators, or FireSim target simulation on AWS F1 cloud FPGAs [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated functional execution or timing-model execution of our mapped target model. The emulator/FPGA implementation is not ASIC signoff. | Target model, emulator/FPGA image, host configuration, workload, and returned traces. |
| Implementation flow | Yosys open-source synthesis [@Yosys], Xilinx Vivado FPGA build flow, and OpenROAD ASIC place-and-route with OpenSTA signoff [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. | Properties exposed by the declared stage, libraries, constraints, modes, and corners. | Every intermediate artifact, tool condition, warning, waiver, and stage result. |

: **Fidelity is relative to the property we are examining.** Our environment retains each tool's model, inputs, conditions, stage, latency, and artifacts instead of collapsing several returns into one generic score. {#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[19,22,29,30]"}

We must carefully weigh cost and property coverage to determine which authorized branches our study can realistically afford to execute. These tool paths differ significantly not only in what they observe, but also in their underlying resource regimes. We can often reconstruct analytical models and compiler checks quite cheaply from our declared inputs. However, our cycle-level (gem5), RTL (Verilator/VCS), and formal (SVA/BMC) runs might prove lengthy, heavily resource-constrained, or even inconclusive. As we move to implementation flows in Yosys, Vivado, and OpenROAD, we take on persistent databases, stage dependencies, and licensed features. Meanwhile, our FireSim FPGA paths introduce complex image or build steps, deployment queues, calibration routines, and the bottleneck of scarce hardware access. To manage this complexity, our environment records the actual realized conditions and costs, rather than trying to infer them from the tool class alone.

ZSim and FireSim clearly illustrate an important operational consequence, where throughput depends on our realized configuration, not just the tool class we choose. In one published setup, ZSim ran a detailed Westmere-class out-of-order model at 20 million simulated instructions per second, roughly $200\times$ slower than the modeled core. That same study noted conventional detailed simulators running at around 200 thousand simulated instructions per second [@ZSim]. FireSim operates in an entirely different regime. When we use FPGA-accelerated simulation, individual target nodes can run at tens to hundreds of megahertz; one notable 1,024-node configuration ran at 3.4\ MHz for 3.2\ GHz targets, achieving a slowdown of less than $1{,}000\times$ [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. We must remember that these rates are merely examples, not universal constants. Our modeled system, host or FPGA allocation, workload, instrumentation, accuracy target, and scale will all shift these numbers. Because of this variability, our environment records the observed throughput alongside its specific conditions, allowing our method to build budgets based on that precisely scoped rate.

SimPoint and SMARTS teach us a separate but equally crucial lesson about sampling identity. While SimPoint helps us select representative program regions, SMARTS provides us with a robust statistical basis for sampled simulation [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Our environment faithfully records our chosen regions, weights, warm-up periods, fast-forward policies, and checkpoint parents. However, it leaves the critical decision of whether those choices actually support our intended comparison entirely up to us.

Maintaining an execution record that retains all transformation, calibration, and version identities alongside branch-specific conditions, we ensure that another architect can seamlessly verify this correspondence.

Let's consider our prospective XR SoC candidate (incorporating an NPU accelerator tile, LPDDR5 memory controller, and L2 cache). Our SRAM and analytical branch receives the precise cache organization and NPU tile configuration along with our declared process, voltage, and temperature conditions. Meanwhile, our compiler and runtime branch (via TVM/LLVM) firmly binds the baseline software image, target NPU features, libraries, flags, and runtime into a uniquely identified binary. Our cycle-level branch (via gem5) then takes that binary and candidate, linking them to our XR workload trace, memory controller traffic generators, cache and power models, warm-up phase, seed, and checkpoint. When we move to RTL simulation in Verilator or VCS, we add our generated RTL, testbench, compile flags, and reset parameters. Our formal checking path (using SVA/BMC) introduces specific named properties such as NoC deadlock-freedom and NPU buffer safety, along with our underlying assumptions, abstraction levels, bounds, and solver details. Logic synthesis in Yosys or Vivado brings in top-level constraints and cell libraries, while our physical implementation step in OpenROAD incorporates the floorplan, process design kit views, operating modes, corners, and any necessary waivers. We must treat these branches as distinct, non-interchangeable paths. In fact, only our screening models and cycle-level simulation branches will participate in the hypothetical fixture we explore later in this chapter. Throughout this process, our environment simply preserves every branch's input, raw and structured returns, costs, conditions, and limits, remaining completely neutral without actively promoting or rejecting our candidate.

Chipyard does an excellent job of making this shared lineage visible. The cited framework explicitly documents the paths leading from a single configuration, through Chisel generation and Flexible Intermediate Representation for RTL (FIRRTL) compiler passes, directly into branch-specific tools for Verilator/VCS RTL simulation, VLSI implementation in OpenROAD, and FireSim FPGA-accelerated simulation [@chipyard]. We should note that our simplified view here doesn't attempt to serve as a definitive map of every Chipyard component or version. Instead, it illustrates how a common configuration supplies the shared lineage, even as our distinct branches produce completely different artifacts and examine separate properties (@fig-chipyard-framework).

![**A common configuration links our distinct authorized tool paths.** This simplified view of the cited Chipyard framework retains configuration lineage while our branch-specific transformations and tools produce artifacts for RTL simulation, VLSI implementation, and FPGA-accelerated simulation [@chipyard].](images/F6b-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework fig-alt="A simplified flow diagram of the Chipyard paths described by the cited framework. A common configuration feeds Chisel generation and compiler transformations. Branch-specific tools then produce artifacts for RTL simulation, a VLSI implementation flow, and FPGA-accelerated simulation."}

Although our common configuration and generated hardware description give us a shared parent, the branch-specific compiler and backend work ultimately dictate which artifact each path consumes and returns. We cannot assume that shared configuration ancestry magically makes branch returns comparable. For any meaningful comparison, we still need carefully matched artifacts, equivalent conditions, and targeted checks for the specific property at issue.

The choice of hardware evaluation environment establishes a fundamental tradeoff between simulation throughput and microarchitectural cycle accuracy (@fig-ch06-simulation-spectrum). Across hardware verification platforms, simulation performance spans seven orders of magnitude, ranging from software RTL simulators (Verilator/VCS executing at $4.5\text{ KIPS}$) to functional ISA emulators (Spike at $48,000\text{ KIPS}$) and analytical models ($8.5\text{ MIPS}$). FPGA-accelerated execution through FireSim occupies a crucial Pareto sweet spot, delivering cycle-exact RTL fidelity ($0\%$ cycle error) at $24,000\text{ KIPS}$, which is over $5,300\times$ faster than software RTL simulation despite requiring a four-hour FPGA compilation build overhead.

![**Simulation speedup versus microarchitectural fidelity spectrum across hardware verification environments.** Evaluation platforms exhibit a wide trade-off between throughput and cycle accuracy, from slow software RTL simulators ($4.5\text{ KIPS}$) to fast functional ISA emulators ($48,000\text{ KIPS}$).
