FireSim FPGA acceleration provides a key Pareto sweet spot, executing cycle-exact RTL at $24,000\text{ KIPS}$ ($0\%$ cycle error), delivering over $5,300\times$ speedup compared to software RTL simulation.](images/fig-ch06-simulation-spectrum.svg){#fig-ch06-simulation-spectrum width="95%" fig-alt="Scatter plot with log-scale horizontal axis showing simulation throughput in KIPS versus microarchitectural cycle error rate on the vertical axis. Bubbles are sized by setup and build overhead time. FireSim FPGA achieves 24,000 KIPS with 0 percent error, VCS RTL simulation achieves 4.5 KIPS with 0 percent error, gem5 achieves 280 KIPS with 4.2 percent error, and Spike achieves 48,000 KIPS with 18.5 percent error."}

While shared lineage successfully identifies related artifacts for us, it doesn't dictate exactly when a branch is ready to run. ArchGym elegantly demonstrates how several architecture simulators can share a common interface under strict, controlled budgets [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. However, our project environment must go a step further. We need it to expose jobs that wait in queues, hold precious licenses, resume from checkpoints, and return results asynchronously, rather than obscuring all of this complex reality behind a single `step()` call.

CHIA gives us a timely, architecture-specific example of an open framework bridging AI-directed hardware/software co-design with heterogeneous tool paths [@CuiEtAl2026CHIA]. Although we can appreciate its concrete integration, the framework alone cannot guarantee that every interface fully preserves our design meaning, securely contains failures, or ensures reproducibility across other projects and tool installations. We must ultimately rely on our overarching project environment to shoulder those heavy responsibilities.

Using a dependency graph, we can clearly identify which branches can run concurrently and which must patiently wait for an input. Modern workflow systems like Nextflow and Snakemake effectively show us how to separate our workflow logic from the actual execution happening on local machines or computing clusters [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow; @KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. As we construct our broader design workflow, our run specification locks in the authorized work, while our harness coordinates everything through a scheduler adapter and backend. In this setup, Nextflow- or Snakemake-style workflow logic merely expresses execution dependencies, it never takes ownership of our design ordering, methodological decisions, results interpretation, or human review processes. Our scheduler might plan the authorized work, but it cannot unilaterally add a new tool, skip a required branch, or change our chosen fidelity level without us issuing a brand new request.

Whenever possible, we should run our inexpensive prerequisite checks before committing to expensive dependent work. If our declared syntax, interface, functional, or SVA/BMC equivalence check discovers that an artifact failed a predeclared prerequisite, our harness immediately records the return and suppresses only the dependent dispatch, stopping the flow well before costly synthesis or physical implementation steps in Vivado or OpenROAD. We don't rely on one rigid, universal tool order; instead, our specifically requested run dynamically determines the exact prerequisites and the branches we can afford to execute.

Our prospective XR SoC application beautifully brings all of these responsibilities together into a single run specification. It seamlessly spans our pinned state, exact translations, tool dependencies, failure handling mechanisms, realized costs, and containment strategies.

## XR SoC Environment

How do environmental containment principles operate when applied to a complex industrial XR SoC evaluation flow? To see how these environmental responsibilities work in practice, we can apply them to a multi-subsystem XR SoC study balancing NPU tile sizing, LPDDR5 memory controller traffic, L2 cache capacity, and gate-level physical synthesis constraints. This example does not represent our complete XR tool graph. Instead, we offer a hypothetical scenario. We selected the thresholds and returned values purely as illustrations, not as empirical tool outputs or historical project data. They do not support any execution fact, validated measurement, comparison, or architecture recommendation.

In our setup, we first pin the candidate and fixed state, and then define the request and return schemas for the screening analytical models (SRAM and NPU area/power) and the cycle-level simulators (gem5 and Verilator). Our run specification explicitly makes simulator dispatch depend on the declared screening returns. It also sets our attempt and time budgets, defines how we authorize resource and license usage, and establishes our reset and retry policy. Once execution completes, our harness retains every return alongside its realized cost.

Before we start any tools, our run specification collects these responsibilities (@tbl-environment-contract). We set up a dispatch condition that authorizes a cycle-level attempt only after complete, schema-valid screening returns meet all designated thresholds. Note that this condition neither validates a measurement nor rejects a candidate on its own.

| **Run category** | **Prospective XR SoC co-design study run specification** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidates and fixed state** | We bind the run specification and study revision to our candidate XR SoC configurations (varying `l2.capacity` between 2\ MiB and 4\ MiB, NPU array dimensions, and memory traffic arbitration). Only declared parameters vary. We keep the CPU core, NoC interconnect, baseline software image, and XR workload trace fixed. Each candidate retains its complete SRAM, NPU tile, memory controller, and technology identity. |
| **Translation and identity** | We serialize declared parameters exactly into analytical screening models under declared process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions, and into eligible gem5/Verilator simulator requests using declared power models. We retain the identity of every behavior-affecting schema, wrapper, parser, tool, model, flag, host or container, seed, and reset state. |
| **Order and dispatch** | We run one screening evaluation per candidate before any dependent cycle-level work. We dispatch cycle-level gem5/Verilator simulations only when screening returns are complete, schemas are valid, combined area is at most $1.5\,\mathrm{mm}^2$, and access latency is at most $2.5\,\mathrm{ns}$. |
| **Matched work and limits** | We run the shared baseline and every eligible alternative under matched conditions. We allow three screening evaluations and at most four cycle-level attempts, including recovery retries. We enforce queue-wait, run-time, and absolute deadlines, stopping when authorized work completes, no alternative qualifies, or a budget expires. |
| **Failures and recovery** | We keep invalid requests, timeouts, cancellations, infrastructure failures, stale state, missing outputs, and parser failures strictly distinct. We link each recovery retry to its parent, charge it against our budget, and regenerate a clean working directory from the fixed state. |
| **Containment and reuse** | We grant access only to declared tools, paths, credentials, networks, and resources. We quarantine output after any unconfirmed termination. We reuse a complete return only when the request, candidate, conditions, translated inputs, tools, wrappers, parsers, and retained artifacts match perfectly. |
| **Returns, cost, and lineage** | We retain SRAM/NPU area, access time, energy, and leakage; matched frame records, LPDDR5 memory traffic inputs, NPU MAC utilization, subsystem power, and warnings; translated inputs, commands, raw logs, parsed outputs, residual artifacts, hashes, resource use, cost, and parent-child lineage. |
| **Decisions left outside** | Our environment does not decide whether a returned value is a valid measurement, whether two returns form a valid comparison, whether a reported limit establishes rejection, or whether a candidate should advance. |

: **This prospective specification illustrates our runtime responsibilities; it is not an executed study record.** We would fix the request, translation, state, expected outputs, failure behavior, cost, and limits before invocation. {#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Our chronology starts with three screening runs. The 2\ MiB rerun baseline, alongside our 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB alternatives, would return combined subsystem areas of $1.2$, $1.4$, and $1.7\,\mathrm{mm}^2$ and access times of $2.1$, $2.4$, and $2.8\,\mathrm{ns}$, respectively. While the first two candidates meet both of our declared thresholds, the 4\ MiB candidate falls short. Consequently, our run specification blocks any dependent cycle-level dispatch for it. Importantly, the values alone would not establish that decision without our verified parse status and recorded dispatch outcome.

Our eligible candidates then enter matched cycle-level runs under the four-attempt budget. The baseline would return a combined subsystem dynamic and leakage power of $2.90\,\mathrm{W}$. If our first 3\ MiB attempt encounters a stale-state setup failure, the harness authorizes a controlled retry from a clean reset, followed by a separate planned repeat. These attempts completely exhaust our budget. Although the recovery retry and planned repeat would return frame, cache, NPU MAC utilization, and power metrics, their specific values remain unreported here. Any summary we derive from them would constitute a new artifact, rather than another tool call.

To be complete, our resulting record must connect the three candidates, their screening returns, the eligible cycle-level work, the failed attempt, the retry and reset links, the planned repeat, every generated artifact, and the total realized cost. In this example, we leave several elements unreported, such as artifact identities, resource use, cost, output lineage, exact translated inputs and hashes, behavior-affecting versions, starting and reset-state identities, seeds and job times, parser and raw-artifact identities, and matched frame records. Because of these omissions, our record remains incomplete under @tbl-environment-contract and the execution-record concept we introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. Later, @sec-feedback-verification-trust determines whether any of our complete returns can become a valid measurement, comparison, or basis for advancing a candidate.

Our harness maintains one exact identity connected across candidate state, translation, execution, reuse, and return. By strictly enforcing our dispatch conditions, budgets, deadlines, and stopping rules, we prevent an eligible candidate from authorizing unlimited work. When we execute a recovery, it consumes our budget while preserving its parent lineage. Meanwhile, our containment and retention policies keep failed or uncertain work fully reviewable without admitting it as a completed return.

We must write this entire specification before making our first tool call. If we fill it in afterward, we cannot definitively refuse a bad translation or demand a missing output. While our specification may authorize dynamic host selection, license reservation, pausing, and resuming, any fundamental change, such as substituting a tool path, serving stale state, or skipping the baseline, requires us to issue an entirely new request.

## Common Architectural Pitfalls

What execution environment pitfalls corrupt simulation lineages and invalidate performance claims? When we connect automated flows to heterogeneous hardware tools, operational failures arise from uncontained state, unhandled timeouts, and silent environment mismatches. We frequently encounter critical pitfalls when executing architecture evaluation tasks across diverse EDA, simulation, and emulation environments.

**Silent Drifts in gem5 Architectural Simulation Configurations.** When we execute cycle-accurate architectural studies in gem5, a full-system architectural simulator, subtle default parameter changes across minor version revisions or unverified Ruby memory hierarchy flags corrupt execution lineage. Automated flows that fail to lock exact gem5 build hashes and seed states produce non-reproducible cache latency and memory contention measurements.

**Unmanaged License Preemption in VCS RTL Simulation Flows.** Running Synopsys VCS, an event-driven RTL simulator, under Slurm, a high-performance computing workload manager, introduces silent job preemptions and license check-out failures. Harnesses that treat license denials as hard design rejections corrupt dataset provenance by masking operational cluster limits as physical hardware incompatibilities.

**Failing to Reset Persistent State in FireSim FPGA-Accelerated Runs.** FireSim, an FPGA-accelerated full-system simulation environment, relies on persistent host DRAM state and FPGA bitstream images across simulation runs. If an execution environment fails to force a hard reset of host memory and PCIe register state between candidate evaluations, residual kernel buffers corrupt subsequent workload timing measurements.

**Silent DRC Violations and Macro Collisions in OpenROAD Physical Design.** OpenROAD, an open-source physical design toolchain, completes floorplanning and placement without automatically stopping on intermediate Design Rule Checking (DRC) errors. Automated environments that parse final area metrics without validating detailed routing reports accept layouts with un-routable signal pin collisions or power grid shorts.

**Stale Memory Map Checkpoints in ZeBu and Palladium Hardware Emulation.** ZeBu and Palladium, enterprise hardware emulation platforms, save execution checkpoints to accelerate long booting sequences. Re-using an emulation checkpoint after modifying register-transfer level memory controllers or bus interfaces silently executes stale memory mappings, invalidating hardware verification results.

**Uncontained Coroutine Deadlocks in Cocotb Python Testbenches.** Cocotb, a Python-based coroutine verification framework, interfaces with RTL simulators through standard procedural interfaces. When testbenches encounter unhandled coroutine exceptions or missing clock edges, Cocotb hangs indefinitely. Harnesses lacking explicit wall-clock timeouts starve Slurm queue allocations and block execution pipelines.

## Open Questions

What open engineering questions challenge tool containment, workflow orchestration, and cross-toolchain semantic alignment? Our environment abstractions separate execution containment from result qualification, but deploying them across shifting tools and security boundaries introduces open engineering questions. We organize these challenges into workflow orchestration, infrastructure failures, and cross-toolchain meaning.

### Workflow Orchestration

- **How do we maintain tool containment as workflow complexity grows?** As our studies invoke dozens of stateful tools across container, cloud, and local environments, maintaining clean execution boundaries without introducing excessive virtualization overhead remains a constant challenge.

### Infrastructure Failures

- **How do we efficiently classify unexpected tool failures at scale?** When thousands of tool runs fail across diverse EDA flows, automatically distinguishing recoverable license timeouts or memory limits from true design illegalities is essential for avoiding corrupted dataset lineage.

### Cross-Toolchain Meaning

- **How can an automated method verify that a tool translation preserves our requested architecture change?** We know basic syntax and type checks easily miss critical errors like silent defaults, rounding issues, unexpected generated collateral, and unsupported tool combinations. Our open research problem is figuring out how to rigorously compare the semantics of an incoming request against the translated artifact, without rigidly rejecting harmless, tool-specific syntax repairs.

- **How can an AI-assisted environment expose semantic differences among tool returns that look operationally alike?** When we combine multi-fidelity tools, matching identities and numeric attributes can mask profound differences in modeled properties, assumptions, units, design stages, and fidelities. Our environment must make these structural differences explicit to the study without unilaterally deciding what architectural claim they actually support.

**Keeping execution valid and contained.** The long-running architecture tools we rely on, especially those in physical design or cycle-level simulation, maintain complex state and demand access to shared files, machines, licenses, and intellectual property. Our environment has to survive failures and state changes without confusing the workflow or quietly expanding its own authority.

- **How can an AI-assisted environment determine that a stateful architecture tool has returned to a valid starting state?** Working directories, persistent databases, caches, checkpoints, random seeds, and host libraries routinely survive restarts. We need robust reset mechanisms that clear influential, run-specific state without paying the overhead of completely tearing down and recreating the tool session for every attempt.

- **How can our environment safely preserve useful partial or delayed tool results after the architecture state changes?** Intermediate data, like an early placement map or a partial simulation trace, often remains diagnostically useful even when it no longer describes our current candidate. If we carelessly reuse this data, we mix incompatible states; if we eagerly discard it, we throw away expensive simulation or physical-design work. We must solve the open problem of tracking what remains semantically valid and carrying its lineage forward, without accidentally admitting it as current evaluation evidence.

- **How can an environment grant an AI system only the exact access needed for one architecture tool action?** The scripts, RTL, constraints, and commands we generate might require specific files, tool binaries, licenses, and host machines, but they rarely need broad system credentials or external network access. As system builders, our challenge is designing strict, dynamically scoped authorization that grants just enough authority for valid work, while effectively containing malformed requests or adversarial actions.

## Conclusion

How do execution environment abstractions elevate tool records into authoritative architectural evidence?

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Elevate execution records to seminal artifacts"}
**Principle:** We elevate environment bindings, execution logs, and replayable run archives into seminal, citation-worthy principles.

**Design Rule:** We treat every execution record and replayable archive as a primary architectural artifact. We must publish environment bindings and execution logs with the same rigor as our final design metrics, ensuring that our claims rest on a fully transparent and verifiable foundation.
:::

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Tool mechanics must not change the design being evaluated"}
**Principle:** Our tool-connected environments must preserve the exact architectural intent across all translations, scheduling operations, retries, and parsing phases.

**Design Rule:** While we allow wrappers to modify file syntax and command structures, and harnesses to manage execution states, they must never silently alter the requested architecture parameters or synthesize a completed return from a failed or partial run. We must retain separate, immutable records covering execution status, raw artifacts, parsed attributes, lineage, and realized costs.
:::

Preserving our requested design is only the first step. The actions that eventually reach our tools must also operate within a recoverable execution boundary.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Automate tool actions only inside a recoverable boundary"}
**Principle:** We must completely contain our tool automation within an isolated, strictly budgeted, and fully observable runtime boundary.

**Design Rule:** We must explicitly define finite budgets for elapsed time, compute, storage, and license usage per attempt. Our cancellation operations have to definitively confirm process termination and resource release, completely quarantining any late-arriving artifacts. Our environment must always be able to cleanly roll back an action or reset to a known-valid state; if we need to take an action with irreversible effects or elevated permissions, we must subject it to an independent authorization gate.
:::

When we deploy a tool, whether it acts as a simulator, a synthesizer, or an analyzer, it transforms an artifact or evaluates a specific property. To manage this safely, we use a wrapper to validate, translate, invoke, and parse that single tool. We then rely on a harness to coordinate attempts, jobs, resources, failures, and execution records across multiple wrappers. Ultimately, our complete environment bridges the gap, connecting our represented study state and permitted actions directly to those tools and their subsequent returns.

Our prospective run specification outlines exactly what we allow to run, detailing the state, authority, and allocated budget. Conversely, the execution record captures what actually ran, what returned, and the real cost incurred. Crucially, neither of these records inherently constitutes a supported architecture claim; we still need subsequent checks to qualify any measurement, comparison, or decision. Maintaining this clear distinction prevents us from erroneously collapsing invalid requests, execution failures, incomplete artifacts, formal outcomes, and design-limit violations into a single ambiguous result. As we evaluate our environments, we must treat exact replay, repeatability, replicability, and reproducibility as separate, distinct claims, remembering that hashes establish pure byte identity rather than semantic equivalence.

We extend this exact same discipline into our multi-tool and multi-fidelity executions. Since fidelity remains relative to a specific property, our branches describe the same candidate only when their translations accurately preserve the relevant architectural meaning. Our environment excels at establishing what we requested, executed, returned, and spent, preserving enough core identity for both replay and reproduction. However, it cannot qualify a measurement, validate a comparison, or recommend a candidate on its own. In @sec-feedback-verification-trust, we tackle this next crucial step, exploring exactly how these returned values and artifacts can transform into genuinely useful feedback.
